title: Onboarding Messaging Pillars (Email + Console Nudges + Retargeting)
author: Soojin Lee
content:
## Purpose
This page defines the **approved messaging pillars** for Redwood Inference onboarding communications across:
- **Lifecycle emails** (welcome → first-success → troubleshooting → next-step)
- **In-console nudges** (activation checklist + contextual banners)
- **Retargeting ads** (LinkedIn/Google) for non-activated signups and recently lapsed users

The goal is consistent, developer-first language that increases:
- **Activation**: first successful production-like inference call (per sprint primary metric)
- **Early retention**: repeat usage in week 1–2

This is intentionally practical: copy blocks you can reuse, claims you can make, and boundaries on what we should avoid.

---

## Target audience and stage
### Primary audience
**Self-serve software engineers and ML engineers** evaluating inference runtime + platform. Common contexts:
- Adding LLM features to an existing product under real latency/cost constraints
- Evaluating open models and serving stacks without wanting to build infra from scratch
- Running quick proof-of-concept that needs to become production-like quickly

### Stage-based messaging emphasis
1) **Pre-activation (first 0–24h)**: remove friction, prove “it works,” show fast path to first success.
2) **Post-activation (24–72h)**: make the next steps obvious (streaming, tracing, cost dashboard, rate limits, retries).
3) **Week 1–2 retention**: demonstrate reliability, observability, and economics (not just a demo).

---

## Messaging pillars (what we stand for)
Use these pillars in priority order. For each channel, you do *not* need all pillars—pick one primary and one supporting.

### Pillar 1 — Performance you can ship: latency + throughput
**Core statement (approved):**
- “Fast, predictable inference—optimized for production latency and throughput.”

**What to say (developer-first):**
- “Lower tail latency with streaming and a runtime built for continuous batching and KV cache management.”
- “Predictable throughput options as you scale (Hosted → Dedicated → Private).”

**Proof points to use (approved; avoid invented numbers):**
- “Redwood-verified performance profiles in the model catalog (hardware + settings documented).”
- “Streaming responses supported across SDKs.”
- “Latency and token-level metrics in Console to diagnose slow paths.”

**Good copy examples:**
- “Get your first successful call in minutes, then turn on streaming to improve perceived latency.”
- “See token-by-token latency in Console so you can tune prompts and routes with real data.”

**Guardrails / what not to imply:**
- Do not claim “fastest” unless a specific public benchmark link is included.
- Avoid hard numeric claims (e.g., “2x faster”) in lifecycle email/ads unless Ethan Wallace has provided the exact substantiation link.

---

### Pillar 2 — Better unit economics: cost visibility + cost controls
**Core statement (approved):**
- “Optimize cost without losing quality—clear levers and measurable impact.”

**What to say:**
- “Token-level cost breakdowns show what you’re paying for.”
- “Levers like caching, batching, quantization profiles, and routing policies.”

**Proof points (approved):**
- “Console surfaces token-level cost and latency breakdowns.”
- “Built-in rate limits and quotas to keep usage predictable.”
- “Workload-aware suggestions via Redwood Optimize (where enabled).”

**Good copy examples:**
- “Turn on caching and see cost impact in your dashboard—no guesswork.”
- “Keep experiments safe with quotas and budgets, then scale when you’re ready.”

**Guardrails:**
- Do not promise specific $/1M token rates in onboarding messages.
- Do not imply billing savings are automatic; describe levers and visibility.

---

### Pillar 3 — Reliability by design: stay online when things go wrong
**Core statement (approved):**
- “Production-grade reliability with fallbacks and operational tooling.”

**What to say:**
- “Graceful degradation: routing and fallback policies help keep your app up.”
- “Operational visibility: tracing hooks, error analysis, alerts.”

**Proof points (approved):**
- “Dedicated capacity options for predictable throughput and isolation.”
- “Fallback policies and rollout controls (canaries/A-B) available via Console.”
- “Audit logs and enterprise controls in Private deployments.”

**Good copy examples:**
- “Set a fallback model policy so you don’t page at 2am when capacity is tight.”
- “Use canaries to roll model changes safely and catch regressions early.”

**Guardrails:**
- Avoid SLA language in self-serve onboarding unless referencing the correct plan/terms.
- Avoid “zero downtime” claims.

---

### Pillar 4 — Deployment flexibility: hosted, dedicated, private (without rewrites)
**Core statement (approved):**
- “One runtime and workflow across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.”

**What to say:**
- “Start hosted, then keep the same interface as your security or latency needs change.”
- “VPC/on-prem options for regulated workloads.”

**Proof points (approved):**
- “Consistent API + config layer across environments.”
- “Private control plane option with customer-managed networking.”

**Guardrails:**
- Do not position Private as ‘simple’ for every team; keep it factual and offer a sales-assisted path.

---

## Proof points library (approved snippets)
Use these verbatim when possible. If you need new proof points, request review from **Soojin Lee + Ethan Wallace**.

### Product capabilities (safe)
- “Streaming responses supported (improves perceived latency for end users).”
- “Token-level latency and cost breakdowns in Console.”
- “Model catalog with Redwood-verified performance profiles.”
- “Rollouts: canary deploys, A/B tests, and fallback policies.”

### Benchmark references (must include link)
- “See benchmarks: [LINK: Redwood Benchmarks / Performance Profiles]”
- “See quickstart + troubleshooting: [LINK: Quickstart docs]”

### Compliance/security references (use carefully; link preferred)
- “VPC/private deployment options for regulated workloads.”
- “Audit logs and key management integrations (plan-dependent).”

---

## Common objections and how to respond
Use the shortest response that addresses the real concern. Do not argue; offer a next step.

| Objection | What they mean | Approved response | Best CTA |
|---|---|---|---|
| “We’re just testing—why do we need a platform?” | Wants a quick POC | “Start with the Hosted API. You’ll get a fast first success, plus the same tooling you’ll want in production (streaming, cost/latency visibility).” | “Copy/paste the hello-inference snippet” |
| “Latency is inconsistent with other providers.” | Worried about tail latency | “We expose token-level latency and support streaming so you can diagnose and improve the experience. If you need predictable throughput, Dedicated is the path.” | “Turn on streaming + view latency breakdown” |
| “Costs are hard to predict.” | Afraid of bill surprises | “We show token-level cost and provide quotas/rate limits. You can set budgets and measure impact of caching/batching changes.” | “Open cost dashboard” |
| “We can self-host an open-source runtime.” | Build vs buy | “Totally viable if you want to operate it. Redwood focuses on production economics + reliability tooling (rollouts, fallbacks, observability) across hosted/dedicated/private.” | “See routing + rollout controls” |
| “We need VPC / data isolation.” | Security/compliance | “Redwood supports Dedicated and Private options with stronger isolation and controls. Let’s confirm your requirements and recommend the right deployment mode.” | “Talk to Sales / Security checklist” |
| “We got stuck on auth / 401 / key permissions.” | Activation blocker | “Most often it’s API key scope or env var mismatch. Here’s the troubleshooting flow and the exact curl to verify.” | “Troubleshoot auth + copy curl” |

---

## Voice and tone (developer-first)
### Principles
- **Be specific**: name the feature and the next action (“Enable streaming,” “View latency dashboard,” “Create an API key”).
- **Respect competence**: assume the reader can integrate; focus on removing friction and unknowns.
- **Show, don’t hype**: anchor to product behaviors and dashboards; minimize adjectives.
- **Short sentences**: especially for ads and banners.

### Reading level / style
- Prefer technical nouns over marketing phrases: “streaming,” “rate limits,” “fallback route,” “token-level metrics.”
- Avoid “revolutionary,” “game-changing,” “best-in-class” unless paired with a concrete proof point.

---

## Do / Don’t language
### Do
- “Get your first successful response (2xx) and then enable streaming.”
- “See token-level latency and cost—debug with real data.”
- “Set fallback behavior so you stay online under load.”
- “Start hosted; move to dedicated/private when you need isolation or predictable throughput.”

### Don’t
- “Instant enterprise-grade AI” (too vague)
- “Guaranteed lowest cost” (unverifiable; varies by workload)
- “Fastest inference platform” (requires benchmark context + substantiation)
- “Fully compliant” (compliance is contextual; use precise terms and link to the right docs)

---

## Claims and substantiation checklist (required for ads + email headers)
Before launch, ensure:
1) **Is the claim measurable?** If yes, include the metric definition or remove the number.
2) **Is there a link?** For anything comparative or performance-related, include the approved benchmark/docs link.
3) **Is plan-dependency clear?** Dedicated/Private/SLA/security features must not be implied for all self-serve users.
4) **Is the claim reversible?** Avoid statements that could be interpreted as a contractual promise.

Escalation for claim review:
- Owner: **Soojin Lee** (PMM)
- Benchmarks: **Ethan Wallace**
- Compliance-sensitive: route through Security/Compliance doc owners if needed

---

## CTA map (use the closest next step)
Prefer CTAs that match the activation funnel events.

| Stage | Primary CTA | Backup CTA |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-activation | “Create API key” / “Run the curl” | “Open Quickstart” |
| First success | “Enable streaming” | “Try SDK example (TS/Python)” |
| Early retention | “View latency & cost dashboard” | “Set a route / create a deployment” |
| High intent | “Add billing to remove limits” | “Invite a teammate” |

---

## Channel guidance
### Lifecycle email
- Keep subject lines concrete: “Your first inference call (copy/paste)” beats “Welcome to Redwood.”
- One primary message + one CTA. Include troubleshooting link when the email is triggered by non-activation.
- Avoid multiple competing CTAs (e.g., docs + blog + webinar).

### Console nudges (checklist + banners)
- Use imperative microcopy: “Create API key,” “Send first request,” “Enable streaming.”
- Avoid multi-paragraph explanations; link out to docs.
- Never shame the user (“You haven’t done X”). Prefer neutral: “Next step: …”

### Retargeting ads
- Choose one pillar per creative. Keep it tight:
  - Latency: “Streaming + token-level latency metrics.”
  - Cost: “See token-level cost; set quotas.”
  - Reliability: “Fallback policies + rollouts.”
- Landing page must match the ad promise (no bait-and-switch).

---

## Ready-to-use copy blocks (approved)
### Short (ads/banners)
- “Ship faster inference: streaming + token-level latency.”
- “See token-level cost. Tune caching/batching with real numbers.”
- “Stay online: routing + fallback policies for production.”

### Medium (email intro)
- “If you’re evaluating models for a real product, the fastest path is: (1) make a successful call, (2) enable streaming, (3) check latency/cost in Console. Here are copy/paste commands to get there.”

### Troubleshooting framing
- “Stuck on auth or 401s? This is usually API key scope or an env var mismatch. Follow this 2-minute checklist and verify with a known-good curl.”

---
